rules: r <= 1.41 and |r − 1| > 0.02: status Amplifying: springs too stiff for this speed, efficiency none.
|r − 1| <= 0.02: status Resonance, T shown as very large.
δ > 2.00 in: note that higher deflection requires engineering review (FanPedia p. 134).
An answer within ±0.02 in of the model deflection is correct; two attempts per challenge.
assumptions: The load is shared equally by the isolators.
Undamped spring and mass; g = 386 in/s² gives the 3.13 constant.
limitations: Real bases load corners unequally; suppliers then choose a spring per corner.
The spring drawing uses an illustrative 4-inch free height; deflections above 3.4 in are drawn at that limit and labelled off scale.

sources: FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, p. 134 (typical spring deflections)

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Commit a calculated deflection before the reveal, then explore how every input moves deflection, natural frequency and isolation
keyQuestions: How much load does each isolator carry?
How far does a spring compress under that load?
Is the fan running fast enough above the springs' natural frequency to be isolated?
commonMisconceptions: Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency (it divides it by 1.41).
Any spring isolates, whatever the fan speed (below a ratio of 1.41 the springs amplify).
Adding isolators adds deflection (more isolators share the load, so each deflects less).
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score shown as 'First-attempt score: n of 3'; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.
